analogy.p: Think of radiation as things thrown at a crowd of people (the atoms). An alpha particle is a **heavy bowling ball**: it knocks into everyone in its path, quickly loses its energy and stops after only a short distance, so it is strongly ionising but short-range. A beta particle is a **fast marble**: it bumps into fewer people, so it travels further. A gamma ray is like a **ghostly beam of light** that nearly always slips between people without touching them, so it travels very far but rarely hits anyone. The analogy breaks down because radiation does not physically bump into atoms: it interacts through electric forces (and, for gamma, by transferring energy to electrons), and a gamma ray can still ionise if it does interact.

bullets: **Radioactive decay** is when an unstable nucleus emits radiation to become more stable; the nucleus changes, not just the electrons.
The decay is **random**: you cannot predict **which** nucleus will decay next or **when**.
**Activity** is the rate at which a source decays, measured in **becquerel (Bq)**; 1 Bq = 1 decay per second.
**Count rate** is the number of decays per second (or minute) detected by a **Geiger–Müller tube** or similar detector.
You must be able to **compare** alpha, beta and gamma in terms of penetration, range in air and ionising power, and to **balance equations**.
The topic links to isotopes, half-life, background radiation, contamination/irradiation and nuclear fission.
core.h: What the specification asks you to know
core.p: AQA 8463 section 4.4.2 asks you to know that some **unstable nuclei** give out radiation to become more stable, and that this is a **random process**. You must know the **four types of nuclear radiation**: **alpha (α), beta (β), gamma (γ) and neutron (n)**, and for each one its **nature**, its **relative ability to ionise**, its **range in air** and its **penetrating power** through materials. You must also be able to **write and balance nuclear equations** for alpha and beta decay, showing the effect on the **mass number** and **atomic number**. It matters because it underpins medical imaging, radiotherapy, smoke detectors, dating of materials, nuclear power and radiation safety.

bullets: **Unstable nucleus**: one that will emit radiation at some time to reach a more stable state.
**Random** = it cannot be predicted when a **particular nucleus** will decay; the chance of decay in the next second is the same for every nucleus of that isotope.
Radioactive decay is a **nuclear** process; chemical reactions only involve the **electrons** around the nucleus.
**Activity** is measured in **becquerel (Bq)**; a source with an activity of 500 Bq has 500 nuclei decaying every second.
Decay emits **ionising radiation** that can be detected by a **Geiger–Müller tube** (clicks) or photographic film (darkens).
When a nucleus has decayed the daughter nucleus may itself be **unstable** and decay further.
core.h: Why nuclei are unstable and radioactive decay is random
core.p: A nucleus is held together by the **strong nuclear force**, but a nucleus with too many neutrons, too few neutrons or too much energy or too many nucleons is **unstable**. An unstable nucleus becomes more stable by **emitting radiation**: this is **radioactive decay**. Each unstable nucleus has a certain probability of decaying in a given time, but **there is no way to tell when a particular nucleus will decay**: it is a **random** process. Because decay happens in the **nucleus**, it is **not affected by temperature, pressure, chemical bonding or any other physical or chemical conditions**. When there are many nuclei, the average behaviour becomes predictable (this leads to half-life).

bullets: **Activity (Bq)** = number of nuclei decaying per second (a property of the **source**).
**Count rate** = number of counts detected per unit time (a property of the **detector and set-up**).
**Background count** is measured with **no source present**; **corrected count rate = measured count rate − background count rate**.
A GM tube produces a **click/electrical pulse each time ionising radiation enters** and ionises the gas inside.
Keep the **distance** and **orientation** of the source and detector the same for fair comparisons.
Always **repeat readings** and take a **mean** because decay is random (counts vary from run to run).
Example: 1.2×10⁶ decays in 60 s means activity = 1.2×10⁶ ÷ 60 = **2.0×10⁴ Bq**.
core.h: Counting decays: activity and count rate
core.p: A source of radioactive material is described by its **activity**: the number of nuclei that decay each second, measured in **becquerel (Bq)**. We cannot detect every decay: a **Geiger–Müller (GM) tube** only counts the radiation that enters the tube, and it gives a **count rate** (counts per second or per minute). The count rate is always less than the activity unless the detector catches all the radiation. The detector also picks up **background radiation** from the surroundings, so you must **subtract the background count rate** to get the count rate from the source alone.

bullets: **Nature**: 2 protons + 2 neutrons = a **helium nucleus** (symbol ⁴₂He or α); charge **+2**, relative mass **4**.
**Ionising power**: **strongest** of the three (very strongly ionising), because it is big and highly charged.
**Range in air**: only a **few centimetres**; **penetration**: stopped by **paper**, thin card, or the dead outer layer of skin.
**Effect on the nucleus**: mass number **−4**, atomic number **−2**; the element changes to one **two places earlier** in the periodic table.

**Danger**: **outside the body** alpha is not very dangerous (it cannot penetrate the skin); **inside the body** (inhaled/swallowed) it is **very dangerous** because it ionises cells over a very short distance.
**Why short range?** It transfers its energy to the many atoms it collides with and ionises, so it quickly runs out of energy.
Emitted from **heavy** nuclei with **too many protons and neutrons**.
core.p: An **alpha particle** is **two protons and two neutrons**, the same as a **helium nucleus**. It is relatively **massive and has a charge of +2**, so it interacts strongly with the atoms it meets: it is **strongly ionising** but loses its energy quickly and so has a **very short range in air** (a few centimetres) and is **stopped by a sheet of paper** or a few centimetres of air or the outer layer of dead skin. Alpha particles are emitted by large unstable nuclei such as **uranium-238, radium-226 and americium-241**. Alpha emission lowers the **mass number by 4** and the **atomic number by 2**.

bullets: **Nature**: a **fast-moving electron** emitted from the **nucleus** (not from the electron shells); symbol ⁰₋₁e or β⁻.
**Process**: **neutron → proton + electron**; the electron is emitted and the proton stays in the nucleus.
**Effect on the nucleus**: mass number **unchanged**, atomic number **+1** (the element changes to the next one along the periodic table).
**Ionising power**: **moderate**; **range in air**: about **1 m** (some sources quote a few metres); **penetration**: stopped by **thin aluminium (a few mm)**.
**Danger**: harmful both outside and inside the body because it can **pass through skin** to some extent.
Emitted by nuclei with **too many neutrons** compared with protons, e.g. **carbon-14** and **strontium-90**.
**Not** the same as an electron in an atom: a beta particle comes from a **nuclear change**.
core.p: A **beta particle** (β⁻) is a **high-speed electron** that is **emitted from the nucleus** when a **neutron changes into a proton**. It has a charge of **−1** and a very small mass (about 1/1840 of a proton). It is **moderately ionising** (less than alpha because it is smaller and moves faster, so it spends less time near each atom), has a range in air of about **a metre** or so, and is **stopped by a few millimetres of aluminium** (not by paper). In beta decay, the **mass number does not change** (a neutron is replaced by a proton, so the total number of nucleons is unchanged) but the **atomic number increases by 1**.

bullets: **Nature**: **high-frequency electromagnetic wave** from the nucleus; **no mass, no charge**; symbol γ.
**Effect on the nucleus**: **no change** in mass number or atomic number (just a **loss of energy**).
**Ionising power**: **weakest** (very weakly ionising) because it rarely interacts with atoms.
**Range in air**: **very long** (many metres or more); **penetration**: reduced by **thick lead or concrete**, never completely stopped.
**Danger**: it **penetrates the body**, so outside and inside sources are both dangerous; useful in **medical tracers** and **sterilising equipment** because it can pass through.
It is called **radiation, not a particle**, so it does not appear as a particle in nuclear equations (but it often accompanies α or β decay).
Gamma rays have the **highest frequency and shortest wavelength** of the electromagnetic spectrum.
core.p: **Gamma rays** are **electromagnetic radiation** of very high frequency emitted from the **nucleus**. They are emitted when a nucleus has **excess energy** after an alpha or beta decay (the daughter nucleus is left in an **excited state**), so gamma emission often follows alpha or beta emission. A gamma ray has **no mass and no charge**, so it is only **weakly ionising**, but it is **very penetrating**: it has a **very long range in air**, passes through paper and aluminium, and is only **reduced** (not stopped) by **thick lead or several metres of concrete**. Emitting gamma changes **neither the mass number nor the atomic number**, but the nucleus **loses energy**.

bullets: **Nature**: a **neutron** (relative mass 1, relative charge 0); symbol ¹₀n.
**Effect on the nucleus**: **mass number −1**, **atomic number unchanged**, so the atom becomes a **different isotope of the same element**.
Neutrons are **released in nuclear fission**, which maintains a **chain reaction** in a nuclear reactor.
They are **very penetrating**; shielding is made from **water or concrete**.
Neutrons can be **absorbed by stable nuclei, making them radioactive** (neutron activation), so materials near a reactor can become radioactive.
At GCSE you mainly need to **recognise neutron radiation as a type of nuclear radiation**; details of its penetration are **extension**, so check your exam board's expectations.
Do not confuse neutron radiation with **alpha** (which contains neutrons but has charge +2).
core.p: A **neutron** (¹₀n) is a neutral particle that can be emitted from some unstable nuclei, and it is also released in **nuclear fission**. AQA expects you to know that **neutron radiation** is one of the types of nuclear radiation. Since a neutron has **no charge**, it does not ionise directly (it ionises indirectly by hitting nuclei, which then ionise) and it is **very penetrating** because it is not repelled by the electrons or the nuclei. It is stopped or slowed by materials rich in **hydrogen** such as **water, concrete or paraffin wax**. When a nucleus emits a neutron, its **mass number falls by 1** and its **atomic number is unchanged**.

bullets: **Alpha**: **+2**, relative mass **4**; **most ionising**; range in air **a few cm**; stopped by **paper**.
**Beta (β⁻)**: **−1**, mass **very small** (≈1/1840); **moderately ionising**; range in air **~1 m**; stopped by **few mm of aluminium**.
**Gamma**: **0**, **no mass**; **weakly ionising**; range in air **very long**; **reduced by thick lead / concrete**.
**Why the inverse link?** Ionising radiation transfers energy by ionising atoms; strongly ionising radiation transfers its energy in a short distance.
**Hazard outside the body**: gamma and beta are more dangerous than alpha; **inside the body**: alpha is most dangerous.
**Absorber test**: place **paper, aluminium, lead** between source and detector; the count rate falling shows which radiation is present.
Always give a **reason** (e.g. 'alpha has a large charge and mass so it ionises many atoms and is absorbed quickly').
core.h: Comparing alpha, beta and gamma: ionisation, range and penetration
core.p: A common exam task is to **compare the three types**. There is an **inverse relationship** between how strongly a radiation ionises and how far it can penetrate: a particle that ionises strongly loses energy quickly, so it does not travel far. Alpha ionises most and penetrates least; gamma ionises least and penetrates most; beta is in between. The diagram shows what is needed to stop each radiation. Use the correct comparative words: 'strongly', 'weakly', 'moderately'.

bullets: **Ionisation**: removal of electrons from atoms to form **ions**; radiation that does this is **ionising radiation**.
**Effects on cells**: damage to **DNA** → **cell death**, **mutation**, **cancer**; large doses cause **radiation sickness**.
**Alpha**: strongly ionising → very dangerous **inside** the body; weak outside.
**Beta and gamma**: can penetrate the skin; **gamma** can pass through the body and affect internal organs.
**Precautions**: use **tongs** to handle sources, keep sources in **lead-lined boxes**, **limit exposure time**, **keep distance**, wear **protective clothing** and **dosimeter badges**.
**Contamination** (radioactive atoms get on or in you) vs **irradiation** (exposed to radiation from a source without contact).
Medical uses depend on penetration: **gamma** tracers for imaging, **gamma** for **radiotherapy**.
core.h: Ionisation and why radiation is dangerous
core.p: **Ionisation** is when radiation **knocks electrons off atoms**, producing **positive ions** and free electrons. In living cells ionising radiation can **damage or kill cells** or damage the **DNA** (causing **mutations** and possibly **cancer**). The danger depends on the **type of radiation**, the **dose**, and whether the source is **inside or outside** the body. Because alpha particles are absorbed within a few centimetres of air or by skin, they are harmless outside the body but very damaging if the source is **inhaled or swallowed**.

bullets: **Mass number (A)** = protons + neutrons (top number); **atomic number (Z)** = protons (bottom number).
**Alpha**: X (mass A, atomic Z) → Y (mass A−4, atomic Z−2) + ⁴₂He; mass number **−4**, atomic number **−2**.
**Beta⁻**: X (mass A, atomic Z) → Y (mass A, atomic Z+1) + ⁰₋₁e; mass number **same**, atomic number **+1**.
**Gamma**: no change in A or Z; the nucleus loses energy only (X* → X + γ).
**Neutron emission**: mass number **−1**, atomic number **same**.
Check: **sum of mass numbers on the left = sum on the right**, and the same for atomic numbers.
Use the **periodic table** to name the new element from its atomic number.
In exams you only need to **balance** equations and use the **symbol of the particle**; you do not need the antineutrino (not in AQA GCSE).
core.p: Nuclear equations show what happens to the **nucleus** in a decay. Each nucleus is written with its **mass number (top)** and **atomic number (bottom)**, for example ²³⁸₉₂U. In every nuclear equation, the **total mass number** and the **total atomic number** must be **the same on both sides** (they are conserved). To balance an equation, add up the top numbers and the bottom numbers on each side and check that they match. The **atomic number identifies the element**, so a change in atomic number means the nucleus has become a **different element**.

bullets: **Alpha decay of U-238**: ²³⁸₉₂U → ²³⁴₉₀Th + ⁴₂He.
**Beta decay of C-14**: ¹⁴₆C → ¹⁴₇N + ⁰₋₁e (the carbon becomes nitrogen).
**Alpha decay of Ra-226**: ²²⁶₈₈Ra → ²²²₈₆Rn + ⁴₂He.
**Beta decay of Sr-90**: ⁹⁰₃₈Sr → ⁹⁰₃₉Y + ⁰₋₁e.
**Missing number type question**: to find an unknown atomic number, make the bottom numbers add up on each side.
**Gamma after alpha**: the new nucleus may be excited, giving a further γ with no change in A or Z.
**Decay chain**: the daughter may itself be unstable and decay again; several decays form a **decay series** that ends in a stable nucleus.
core.h: Worked equations: alpha and beta decay
core.p: Here are the key examples to know. **Uranium-238** emits an alpha particle to become **thorium-234**: ²³⁸₉₂U → ²³⁴₉₀Th + ⁴₂He. Check: 238 = 234 + 4 and 92 = 90 + 2. **Carbon-14** (used in radiocarbon dating) emits a beta particle to become **nitrogen-14**: ¹⁴₆C → ¹⁴₇N + ⁰₋₁e. Check: 14 = 14 + 0 and 6 = 7 + (−1). **Radium-226** decays by alpha emission to **radon-222**: ²²⁶₈₈Ra → ²²²₈₆Rn + ⁴₂He. Check: 226 = 222 + 4 and 88 = 86 + 2. **Strontium-90** emits a beta particle to become **yttrium-90**: ⁹⁰₃₈Sr → ⁹⁰₃₉Y + ⁰₋₁e (90 = 90 + 0; 38 = 39 − 1).

bullets: Measure the **background count first** (no source) and **subtract** it from every reading.
Keep **distance, time interval and detector position** the same each time (**control variables**).
**Repeat** each measurement and use a **mean** because radioactive decay is random.
**Interpreting data**: count falls to background with **paper** → **alpha**; falls with **aluminium** → **beta**; stays high with aluminium but falls with **lead** → **gamma**.
A source may emit **more than one type** (e.g. beta and gamma), so look at **how the count falls** with each absorber.
**Safety**: handle the source with **tongs**, point it away from people, store in a lead-lined box, and keep **time of use short**.
Alpha has a very short range, so the **source must be very close to the detector** (or in a vacuum) to detect it.
core.p: Radiation cannot be seen, so we detect it by the **ionisation** it causes. A **Geiger–Müller tube** has a gas that is ionised when radiation enters and produces a **pulse of current** that the counter records as a click or count. **Photographic film** also detects radiation because it **darkens** when exposed. To work out which type of radiation a source emits, place **different absorbers** between the source and the detector at a fixed distance and see how the **corrected count rate** changes: if paper blocks it, it is alpha; if aluminium blocks it, it is beta; if only thick lead reduces it, it is gamma.

bullets: **Half-life**: time for the **number of unstable nuclei** (or activity) to **halve**; follows from random decay.
**Background radiation**: always present; must be **subtracted** from readings.
**Uses**: gamma tracers (penetrate the body), beta in **thickness gauges**, alpha in **smoke detectors**.
**Contamination vs irradiation**: how radiation exposure happens.
**Nuclear fission**: a neutron causes a large nucleus to split and release more neutrons.
**Atomic structure**: protons, neutrons, isotopes; decay changes the **numbers of protons and neutrons**.
**Electromagnetic spectrum**: gamma rays are at the high-frequency end.
core.p: This spec point leads to several others in 4.4. **Half-life** describes the time for the activity (or number of unstable nuclei) to halve and uses the fact that decay is random. **Background radiation** (from rocks, cosmic rays, medical, nuclear fallout and radon gas) must be corrected for in all measurements. **Uses of radioactive materials** (smoke alarms, medical tracers, thickness gauges, radiotherapy, sterilisation) depend on the penetrating power and half-life. **Nuclear fission and fusion** involve neutrons and nuclear changes. Finally, **isotopes** and **atomic structure** (including the models from the previous spec point) are needed to understand what changes in a decay.

bullets: **State** the type of radiation **and** give a **reason** (e.g. 'alpha, because it is stopped by paper').
**Don't say** 'alpha has the highest penetrating power'; say **'alpha is the most ionising but the least penetrating'**.
**Write** the **atomic number and mass number** clearly; mark schemes separate them.
**Quote specific materials**: paper (alpha), 3 mm aluminium (beta), several cm lead/metres concrete (gamma).
**Relate hazards to the situation**: alpha is dangerous **inside** the body; gamma/beta dangerous **outside** too.
For '**explain**' questions use because/so: 'it is strongly ionising **so** it loses its energy quickly **so** it has a short range'.
core.p: Questions on radiation types are usually 1–4 marks for recall and comparison, and sometimes a 6-mark question asking you to evaluate the use of a source or to describe an investigation. Use the **correct terms** (ionising, penetrating, range, stopped by) and **always compare** (e.g. 'alpha is more strongly ionising than beta'). For equations, **show the check** that the top and bottom numbers balance, because marks are often awarded for the correct mass number and atomic number separately.

exam: **State/Name** (1 mark): give the type (alpha, beta, gamma) and, if asked, **a reason** (e.g. stopped by paper).
**Compare** (2–3 marks): use **comparative words** — 'more', 'less', 'strongly', 'weakly' — for **ionising power, range, and penetration**.
**Explain why alpha has a short range** (2 marks): strongly ionising **so** it loses energy quickly **so** it is stopped in a few cm of air.
**Nuclear equations** (usually 2–3 marks): one mark for each correct **mass number** and **atomic number**, and one for the correct **symbol/element**.
**Check your equation**: top numbers add up on both sides; bottom numbers add up on both sides.

**Describe an investigation** (4–6 marks): measure **background**, put source at a **fixed distance**, add **paper, aluminium, lead**, record **count rate**, **subtract background**, **repeat** and **mean**.
**Data questions**: if the count rate falls to the background level when a material is added, that radiation is **fully absorbed**; if it falls but not to background, some radiation **penetrates**.
**Safety questions**: tongs, distance, short time, shielding, storing in lead-lined box, never pointing a source at people.
**Hazard questions**: link the **type** and **location** (inside/outside body) with the damage it could do (**ionisation → DNA damage → cancer**).
**Use correct unit**: activity in **Bq**, count rate in **counts per second (or min)**.

mistakes.r: Alpha is the **most ionising** but **least penetrating**; it is stopped by paper.
mistakes.w: Alpha is the most penetrating because it is the biggest.

mistakes.r: Gamma is **reduced** by thick lead or concrete; it is **never completely stopped**.
Beta particles come from the **nucleus**, when a **neutron changes into a proton and an electron**.
mistakes.w: Beta particles come from the electron shells.

mistakes.r: In beta decay the **mass number stays the same** and the **atomic number goes up by 1**.
mistakes.w: In beta decay the mass number goes down.

mistakes.r: In alpha decay the **mass number falls by 4** and the **atomic number falls by 2**.
mistakes.w: In alpha decay the atomic number falls by 4.

mistakes.r: Radioactive decay is **random** and is **not affected** by temperature, pressure or chemical conditions.
mistakes.w: Radioactive decay is faster if the substance is heated.

mistakes.r: **Activity** (Bq) is the decays per second of the source; **count rate** is only what the **detector** records, and it must be **corrected for background**.
mistakes.w: The count rate is the same as the activity.

mistakes.r: Alpha is **not very dangerous outside** (absorbed by skin) but **very dangerous inside** the body.
mistakes.w: Alpha particles are dangerous outside the body.

summary: The spec asks you to know that unstable nuclei emit alpha, beta, gamma or neutron radiation at random, and to describe each type's nature, ionising power, range in air and penetration, and to write balanced nuclear equations for alpha and beta decay. It matters because the properties of each radiation decide how it can be used safely in medicine, industry and power.

terms.d: The spontaneous change of an unstable nucleus, which emits radiation to become more stable; a random process.
A nucleus that will emit radiation at some time to become more stable.
Cannot be predicted: it is not known when a particular nucleus will decay.
The rate at which a source of unstable nuclei decays, measured in becquerel (Bq).
The unit of activity; 1 Bq is one decay per second.
The number of decays recorded by a detector (such as a GM tube) per second or per minute.
Low-level ionising radiation always present from natural and man-made sources; must be subtracted from readings.
Two neutrons and two protons (a helium nucleus), emitted from the nucleus; strongly ionising, short range, stopped by paper.
A high-speed electron emitted from the nucleus when a neutron changes into a proton; stopped by thin aluminium.
Electromagnetic radiation emitted from the nucleus; weakly ionising, very penetrating, reduced by thick lead or concrete.
Neutrons emitted from some unstable nuclei or released in fission; uncharged and very penetrating.
The process of removing electrons from atoms, producing positive ions.
Radiation (alpha, beta, gamma, neutrons, X-rays) that can remove electrons from atoms.
How far radiation can pass through a material before being absorbed.
The total number of protons and neutrons in a nucleus.
The number of protons in a nucleus; it identifies the element.
An equation showing a nuclear change, in which mass number and atomic number are both balanced.
A detector in which ionising radiation produces pulses of current that are counted.

worked.ans: ²³⁸₉₂U → ²³⁴₉₀Th + ⁴₂He. The thorium nucleus has **mass number 234** and **atomic number 90**.
worked.q: Uranium-238 (atomic number 92) decays by emitting an alpha particle to form thorium. Write a balanced nuclear equation and state the mass number and atomic number of the thorium nucleus. (3 marks)
steps: An alpha particle is ⁴₂He: mass number 4, atomic number 2.
Atomic number of thorium = 92 − 2 = 90 (this matches thorium on the periodic table).
Write it as ²³⁸₉₂U → ²³⁴₉₀Th + ⁴₂He and check that 238 = 234 + 4 and 92 = 90 + 2.

worked.ans: ⁹⁰₃₈Sr → ⁹⁰₃₉Y + ⁰₋₁e. The new element is **yttrium-90** (atomic number 39), formed because a neutron changed into a proton.
worked.q: A nucleus of strontium-90 (⁹⁰₃₈Sr) decays by beta-minus emission. Give the nuclear equation and name the new element. (3 marks)
steps: A beta-minus particle is ⁰₋₁e: mass number 0, atomic number −1.
Atomic number of new nucleus = 38 − (−1) = 39, which is yttrium (Y).

worked.ans: The source emits **beta radiation only**. The corrected count rate (240 per minute) is not reduced by **paper**, so there is **no alpha**, but it falls to almost **background** (1 per minute) with **3 mm of aluminium**, so it is **beta**; nothing is left to be reduced by lead, so there is **no gamma**.
worked.q: A student has a radioactive source and a GM tube. The background count rate is 5 counts per minute. With no absorber the count rate is 245 counts per minute. With a sheet of paper it is 244, with 3 mm of aluminium it is 6, and with 5 cm of lead it is 5. Which radiations does the source emit? Explain your answer. (4 marks)
steps: Subtract background: no absorber = 245 − 5 = 240; paper = 239; aluminium = 1; lead = 0.
Paper hardly reduces the count (239 ≈ 240), so alpha is not present (alpha would be stopped by paper).
Aluminium reduces the count to almost background, so the radiation is stopped by a few mm of aluminium, which suggests beta.
Lead reduces to background, but aluminium had already removed almost all of it, so there is no significant gamma.
